newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Ockham deals highlights change at Lloyd's.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Ockham deals highlights change at Lloyd's.

text.p: The sale by Lloyd's insurance group Ockham Holdings of its non-core business Bermuda's Ace Ltd marked two factors - a bid by a loss-hit company to reinvent itself, and the evolution of corporate finance behind Lloyd's of London.

For Ockham the 19.5 million stg sale, coupled with a 21 million stg cash injection from U.S. investors led by influential merchant banker Dan Lufkin's Questor group, was a landmark in its recovery plan.
The insurer, formerly known as Sturge, was one of those worst hit during the years 1988-1992 when Lloyd's of London was ravaged by losses. Sturge losses were estimated at over one billion stg.

In 1994 it brought in Lord David Poole, the 51-year-old former stockbroker who was UK prime minister John Major's policy unit industrial supremo for two years, and embarked on a recovery plan which involved forming a new holding company to distance new business from old liabilities, a 21 million stg contribution to the Lloyd's settlement reconstruction and renewal plan, and a re-evaluation of its business lines.
Its conclusion will no doubt worry other insurers facing the same difficulties.
"It was clear that with the huge companies now operating in the international market we would find it very difficult to compete," said Poole.

It decided to concentrate in the short term on building on its 'Highway' operation insuring non-standard motoring risks, a separate market from the mainstream business targeted by companies such as Direct Line.

In the longer term it hopes to use the newly-released cash to research and exploit new opportunities in the financial sector, but insurance analysts on Thursday were slightly disappointed that there was no clearer direction on new business plans.

"Lord Poole thinks that the wait for the Lloyd's profit commissions gives them the luxury of time to think what to go into next," said Roman Cyzdin, insurance analyst at Merrill Lynch. "But the stockmarket has a way of getting restless and it may end up kicking him into doing something," he said.

For Ace, one of the new breed of insurers which have grown up in Bermuda at the expense of traditional insurers, the deal makes it the second largest managing agency at Lloyd's, having bought a majority interest in the Methuen Group at Lloyd's earlier this year.

Ace gains the old Sturge Aviation agency, which will enhance its current aviation insurance operation, and Ockham Worldwide. In 1996 the seven Lloyd's syndicates these agencies manage had an underwriting capacity of 349 million stg, and profit commissions from 1993 (which Ockham will keep under the deal) were in the region of 25 million stg .
Analysts expect Ace to realise the value Ockham has built up in these businesses.
But Ace achieves a bigger goal by becoming a major force at Lloyd's, and it has encouraged the view held by many that the traditional structure of the 300-year-old market is on its last legs.

They predict that before long and that before long the traditional Names who have supported the market will be a thing of the past, and that the market will evolve into an umbrella for a small group of insurance companies working under the Lloyd's banner.

Lloyd's analyst Charles Sturge said: "Lloyd's will very likely become a group of insurers because of pressure from managing agents, who are keen to get as much corporate capital as they can because it is easier to administer and because it is permanent, it is more transparent,"
"If this happens, then obviously the days of individual Names with unlimited liability are numbered. The two types can hardly live together," he said. --Reuters Insurance News +44 171 542 2770
